questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,2]\times [0,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)={x}^{2}y-2x-{y}^{2}+1. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,1]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}=[$ $1.25$ $]$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y-2x-{y}^{2}+1) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y-2x-{y}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy-2) & \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-2) & \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -2\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ 2x & -2\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}2xy-2 \\ {x}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2(1) & 2(1) \\ 2(1) & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}2(1)(1)-2 \\ (1)^{2}-2(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2\cdot (-2)-2\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{8}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1.25 \\ 0.75\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [0,1]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}y-4x+2{y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}. $$ Fill in the blanks in the matrix equation below that defines the first iteration of the Newton-Raphson process starting at the point $[1,\,1]^{T}.$
$[$ {{field-1}} $10$ $]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0})\,=[$ $-6$ $]$
$10$ {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

Equivalently, at each iteration, the above equation can be rewritten as

$$
{H}_{f}({x}_{n})({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-∇f({x}_{n}).
$$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}y-4x+2{y}^{3}-6{y}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}y-4x+2{y}^{3}-6{y}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10xy-4 \\ 5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(10xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(10xy-4) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10y & 10x \\ 10x & 12y-12\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson system of equations is

$$
{[\begin{aligned}10y & 10x \\ 10x & 12y-12\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}({x}_{n+1}-{x}_{n})=-{[\begin{aligned}10xy-4 \\ 5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{[\begin{aligned}10y & 10x \\ 10x & 12y-12\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-{[\begin{aligned}10xy-4 \\ 5{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}-12y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\ [\begin{aligned}10(1) & 10(1) \\ 10(1) & 12(1)-12\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =-[\begin{aligned}10(1)(1)-4 \\ 5(1)^{2}+6(1)^{2}-12(1)\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}10 & 10 \\ 10 & 0\end{aligned}]({x}_{1}-{x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Suppose we wish to find a critical point of the function $f(x,y)$ in the region $[0,1]\times [1,2]⊆{R}^{2},$ where $$ f(x,y)=3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}+2xy-3x. $$ Calculate one iteration of the Newton-Raphson process for optimization that starts at ${x}_{0}=[1,\,2]^{T}.$ Round your final answer to three decimal places (if needed).
${x}_{1}≈[$ $0.375$ $]$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}+2xy-3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}y-{x}^{2}+2xy-3x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6xy-2x+2y-3 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy-2x+2y-3) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+2x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy-2x+2y-3) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+2x)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6y-2 & 6x+2 \\ 6x+2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}6y-2 & 6x+2 \\ 6x+2 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}6xy-2x+2y-3 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}6y-2 & 6x+2 \\ 6x+2 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}6xy-2x+2y-3 \\ 3{x}^{2}+2x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6(2)-2 & 6(1)+2 \\ 6(1)+2 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}6(1)(2)-2(1)+2(2)-3 \\ 3(1)^{2}+2(1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}10 & 8 \\ 8 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{10\cdot 0-8\cdot 8}[\begin{aligned}0 & -8 \\ -8 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}11 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{64}[\begin{aligned}-40 \\ -38\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}0.375 \\ 1.406\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

${x}_{1}≈[$ $1.014$ $]$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}-x+3{y}^{2}+3) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2}-x+3{y}^{2}+3)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6xy-2{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(6xy-2{y}^{2}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(6xy-2{y}^{2}-1) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6y & 6x-4y \\ 6x-4y & 6-4x\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}6y & 6x-4y \\ 6x-4y & 6-4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}6xy-2{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}6y & 6x-4y \\ 6x-4y & 6-4x\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}6xy-2{y}^{2}-1 \\ 3{x}^{2}-4xy+6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}6(0) & 6(2)-4(0) \\ 6(2)-4(0) & 6-4(2)\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}6(2)(0)-2(0)^{2}-1 \\ 3(2)^{2}-4(2)(0)+6(0)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 12 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2)-12\cdot 12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -12 \\ -12 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}-142 \\ 12\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}1.014 \\ 0.083\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

${x}_{1}≈[$ {{field-1}} $]$
{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
The Newton-Raphson method of optimizing a multivariable function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-[{H}_{f}({x}_{n})]^{-1}∇f({x}_{n}),
$$

where $H({x}_{n})$ and $∇f({x}_{n})$ are the Hessian and gradient of $f$, respectively, evaluated at ${x}_{n}.$

In our case, the gradient is

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}y-2{x}^{2}+xy-3{y}^{2}-2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and the Hessian is

$$
\begin{aligned}{H}_{f}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂x}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y) \\ \frac{∂}{∂y}(8xy-4x+y) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{2}+x-6y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our Newton-Raphson formula is

$$
{x}_{n+1}={x}_{n}-{[\begin{aligned}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{n}}.
$$

Starting with
${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{0}-{[\begin{aligned}8y-4 & 8x+1 \\ 8x+1 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}}^{-1}{[\begin{aligned}8xy-4x+y \\ 4{x}^{2}+x-6y\end{aligned}]}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}8(2)-4 & 8(1)+1 \\ 8(1)+1 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}8(1)(2)-4(1)+2 \\ 4(1)^{2}+(1)-6(2)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-{[\begin{aligned}12 & 9 \\ 9 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}14 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{12\cdot (-6)-9\cdot 9}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -9 \\ -9 & 12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}14 \\ -7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{153}[\begin{aligned}-21 \\ -210\end{aligned}] \\  & ≈[\begin{aligned}0.863 \\ 0.627\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
